messages.subject: Mixture model (beta/binomial + gamma)
parts:
[There's a post by Andrew Gelman on this subject here, with code by Bob Carpenter, so I'm sure it can be done, but how it can be done is not clear to me]
Suppose I try to model x using a mixture model: there's a P probability that x equals zero, and (1 - P) probability that x follows a gamma distribution with shape parameter S and rate parameter R. For example:

sample_size = 1E5
P = 0.95
S = 1
R = 0.1
x = rbinom (sample_size, 1, 1 - P) * rgamma (sample_size, S, R)

What does my Stan model have to look like in order to estimate P, S, and R? I assume I have to do it using target += ... but I don't know how.
Thanks!

messages.author: b1e64236b865525c
messages.subject: Re: Mixture model (beta/binomial + gamma)
parts: My problem's somewhat similar to what Richard McElreath described here. I called it a [m]ixture model beta/binomial+gamma, but zero-inflated gamma is probably a more precise term.

messages.author: b1e64236b865525c
messages.subject: Re: Mixture model (beta/binomial + gamma)
parts:
According to the reference manual,
Zero inflation and hurdle models can be formulated for discrete distributions other than the Poisson. Zero inflation does not work for continuous distributions in Stan because of issues with derivatives; in particular, there is no way to add a point mass to a continuous distribution, such as zero-inflating a normal as a regression coefficient prior.
So I guess I can't do what I want...?

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Mixture model (beta/binomial + gamma)
parts:
On Monday, December 26, 2016 at 7:20:48 PM UTC-5, Vítor Margato wrote:
According to the reference manual,
Zero inflation and hurdle models can be formulated for discrete distributions other than the Poisson. Zero inflation does not work for continuous distributions in Stan because of issues with derivatives; in particular, there is no way to add a point mass to a continuous distribution, such as zero-inflating a normal as a regression coefficient prior.
So I guess I can't do what I want...?

No derivatives are calculated for observed data that you condition on. So, I think a Bernoulli likelihood for whether x > 0 combined a Gamma likelihood for the positive observations would be okay as long as the shape parameter was greater than 1.

messages.subject: Re: Mixture model (beta/binomial + gamma)
parts:
On Monday, December 26, 2016 at 8:22:37 PM UTC-5, Vítor Margato wrote:
Thanks! But... well, the thing is I really don't know how to code the model chunk.
I've looked for instructions (reference manual, other threads, Gelman's blog...?) but couldn't find anything I could understand (admittedly I'm really a Stan beginner).

You should probably start by learning the Stan language and the NUTS algorithm, rather than diving in with some zero-inflated Gamma but here

data {
  int<lower=1> N;
  int<lower=0, upper=1> y[N];
  real<lower=0> x[sum(y)];
}
parameters {
  real<lower=0, upper=1> P;
  real<lower=0> S;
  real<lower=0> R;
}
model {
  target += bernoulli_lpmf(y | 1 - P);
  target += gamma_lpdf(x | S, R);
  // priors
}

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Mixture model (beta/binomial + gamma)
parts:
Look for the zero-inflated Poisson and for mixture models.
You want to be thinking about this as a mixture and
thinking generatively about it. First there's a bernoulli trial
to decide whether to generate 0, and if that is a success you
generate 0 and otherwise draw from a gamma. Then work backward
from that generative model to the likelihood.

- Bob
